title: Three kinds of word: noun, verb, adjective
summary: Almost every Japanese word is a noun, a verb or an い-adjective, and the special kinds of noun each have just one extra power.

blocks.text: Textbooks pour Japanese words into English boxes (adverb, adjective, preposition) and the confusion never ends. The course makes it much simpler: nearly every word is a **noun**, a **verb** or an **adjective**. Besides those there are the **particles**, which are the nuts and bolts, and a handful of real connecting words such as けど.
Verbs and adjectives are easy to spot

A verb always ends in an **う-row kana** (う, く, す, る, ...). An adjective always ends in the kana **い**. Both must show that ending in kana, never inside a kanji. These last kana are the part that changes: 食べる becomes 食べた, 高い becomes 高かった.
So if a word has none of those endings, it is a **noun**. A word written only in kanji is a noun about 99 times out of 100. Japanese is a very **noun-centered** language.
Some nouns have exactly one power that ordinary nouns lack. Each group is still a noun. Everything else about it is plain noun behavior.

rows: may use the soft copula **な** before a noun
する noun (textbook: する verb)
may drop を and fuse with する
may drop the に it would normally need

blocks.text: Any ordinary noun that suits the meaning can become an adverb by adding に. An adverbial noun like ゆっくり simply may leave it out. Without する, a word like 勉強 is still just a noun, which is why 勉強が好きだ works with no verb in sight.

blocks.jp: 静かな部屋で勉強する。
電車がゆっくり止まった。

blocks.en: (I) like study. (the noun, no する needed)

blocks.text: Watch out for あまり and ずいぶん

あまり is a noun meaning "excess" and ずいぶん is a noun meaning "a fair amount". Japanese often says less than it means (understatement). あまり食べない literally says "I do not eat an excess" and in practice means "I do not eat much". ずいぶん上手だ says "you are skilled enough" and means "very skilled".

items: Nearly every word is a **noun**, **verb** or **adjective**.
Verbs end in an **う-row kana**; adjectives end in **い**; anything else is a noun.
Adjectival nouns, する nouns and adverbial nouns are still nouns, each with one extra power.
Words that dictionaries call adverbs are nearly always nouns used without に.

questions.instruction: What kind of word is this?
questions.note: It is written only in kanji and has no verb or adjective ending.

questions.instruction: What kind of word is this?
questions.note: It ends in the kana い, so it is an adjective.

questions.instruction: What kind of word is this?
questions.note: It ends in an う-row kana, so it is a verb.

questions.prompt: 綺麗 (as in 綺麗な花) is a kind of adjective.
questions.note: It is an adjectival noun: a noun that may take な.

questions.instruction: Which noun may drop を and fuse with する?
questions.note: 勉強 is a する noun: 勉強をする becomes 勉強する.
An adjectival noun uses the soft copula な before a noun.
食べた is the only word with a verb ending; the others are nouns with particles.
高い ends in い and stands as the engine.

questions.instruction: What is the superpower of an adverbial noun like ゆっくり?
options: It may drop the に used to make adverbs
It may take the soft copula な
questions.note: ゆっくりにする and ゆっくりする both work.

questions.instruction: What does あまり食べない really say, word for word?
options: I do not eat an excess
questions.note: あまり means excess; the understatement means "not much".

questions.prompt: (I) studied in the library, quietly. (place first, then manner)
questions.note: Place, then manner, then the verb engine at the end.
勉強 is already a noun, so が can follow it directly.
